classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the local direction at the North Pole and on returning to Singapore, then combine three right-angle turns and convert to revolutions.

content.prompt: Suppose that you make a journey on the surface of the globe. You start facing east at Singapore, which lies on the Equator. Then you walk east one-quarter of the way around the globe, then turn $90^{\circ}$ north and walk to the North Pole, then turn $90^{\circ}$ towards Singapore and walk back to Singapore, and finally turn facing east just as you started. Through how many revolutions have you turned during this journey, and what is the sum of the exterior angles of your triangular path? Count clockwise turns as negative and anticlockwise turns as positive.

inlines.text: of a positive revolution; exterior-angle sum
The three local turns are each anticlockwise through a right angle.

answer.worked:
The turn from east to north is $90^{\circ}$ anticlockwise. At the North Pole, the return meridian to Singapore is a quarter-turn from the incoming meridian, so this turn is also $90^{\circ}$ anticlockwise. On returning to Singapore, you face south; turning to face east is another $90^{\circ}$ anticlockwise.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Total turn}&=90^{\circ}+90^{\circ}+90^{\circ}\\\text{Total turn}&=270^{\circ}\\\text{Number of revolutions}&=\frac{270^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}}\\\text{Number of revolutions}&=\frac34.\end{align*}$$

Thus you turn through $\tfrac34$ of a positive revolution, and the sum of the exterior angles is $270^{\circ}$. The path lies on a sphere, so the exterior-angle sum for a convex plane polygon does not apply.
